utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone in this new courtroom environment, which I hope is not going to cause us any technical problems, although everything is new. One of the things I noticed that my priority button disappeared but since in the Krajisnik case I had to use it only once, there seems to be no problem for the time being. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. I'd like to start with two matters, the first one being the admission of the exhibits that have been tendered through the witness, Mr. Pasic. Mr. Registrar has distributed a list of exhibits. I do have technical problems now already. My earphone is not constant in. Okay. Let's see what -- The Registrar has distributed a list of exhibits. Whenever I speak, and I hope the same doesn't happen to you, the sound of my earphones disappears for just a fraction of a second. Could we just test whether a similar thing happens when you speak? Mr. Harmon may I ask you to speak a few words.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This is my turn to experiment, Your Honour. It doesn't seem to be happening to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me just ask whether there is another earphone available or whether it's a structural problem. Let me just see. Same thing happens so it must be the system rather than the earphone. I'll try to survive and see whether something can be done about it in the first break. The list distributed by Mr. Registrar starts at P1024, so 1024, and goes up to 1033.1. Mr. Josse, is there any objection against admission in evidence of any of these documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I object to P1031.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 1031. That's the excerpts from the book, It Is a Crime to Forget a Crime. Is that ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For the reasons?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, my learned friend put one extremely small passage in that book to the witness. He simply asked the witness to adopt the fact that his name effectively appeared in the book, having appeared -- having attended a meeting. That can't be a proper basis for admission of the exhibit, in my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I introduced that exhibit to attempt to refresh the witness's recollection. It did not refresh his recollection. I have no objection to it being removed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you withdraw P1031.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do not know, Mr. Registrar, whether we would leave that number open or whether we would use it again, because it would disturb a bit the sequence of the presentation of evidence if we would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We will move up. That means that 1031 will now be what appears on the list as 1032, that is the regular combat report of the 9th of June. Then 1033 will then be -- on the list will then be 1032. So it just moves up. Then the Chamber decides that the exhibits ranging from P1024 up to and including P1032 are admitted into evidence. Mr. Harmon, tab 26 and tab 27 did not yet receive an exhibit number. Mr. Registrar, would you --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 26, Your Honours, which was the regular combat report dated 15 June 1992 would be given Prosecution Exhibit number P1033. Tab 27, which was the article quoting Jean-Claude Concolato would be given Prosecution Exhibit P1034.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Any objections, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: As far as 1034 is concerned, I take exactly the same point. Didn't -- the witness didn't accept a word that was in the article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We would, Your Honour, request that it be admitted. It is for the Court to give it whatever weight it feels appropriate. It directly contradicted the witness and it's again up to the Chamber to make a decision as to what weight it should be -- it should receive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could at least before we give a decision on this matter, receive a bit more information about where the document stems from, who obtained it, when it was obtained, et cetera, et cetera, so that we have at least some assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I may be able to assist the Chamber now with that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you may do it. If you've got it there, then please tell us. If not, we'll hear from you at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll make submissions on that later. This is an associated press article. That's what I can tell you. It was from the wire service. Where we precisely received it and when we received it I will submit to the Chamber but that's -- the source of the information is the associated press.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Well, as you know, Mr. Harmon, this is not a trial by media, but a trial by hearing witnesses, et cetera, so the Chamber is always very cautious if it comes to press reports although it has not denied admission of it. But at least we should have proper information whether it was obtained by whom it was obtained and -- so we'll hear from you. Mr. Harmon, there was no objection by the Defence but you offered, since the P1024 was not -- that's the Holiday Inn receipt, was not complete or there was some confusion about that, that you would provide us at least with a new copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have those in hand, Your Honour, and I can provide you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse if there would be any problem with them, the decision of the Chamber could be reversed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I say, the Court will find that generally, when I'm sitting in this chair, that type of thing, in other words, the document isn't quite complete, that won't be a ground of objection that I will take.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: My grounds of objection will be exactly along the lines that I've hitherto taken. I won't take technical points like that in general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I take it, Mr. Josse, that you do understand that if the Chamber is provided with evidence that it would like to have a consistent set of documents and complete set of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I wasn't in any way undermining anything that you -- the Court says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I did not understand your observation to mean that it's not important to have full and complete and consistent sets.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I wasn't suggesting that. I understand the Court's concern and I understand the registry's concern but our concern, defending, can often be slightly different for understandable reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand. Then I think, Mr. Harmon, tab 17 I failed to identify the quoted portion in it and you said that you would check what was under tab 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We have distributed a new copy for Your Honour. We did that yesterday. It is tab -- the document in tab 17 was Prosecution Exhibit 739, I'm told.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it was 1st of June rather than the 9th of June, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It is the 1st of June, Your Honour, that's correct, the 1st of June 1992. It's a 1st Krajina Corps report on the current political and security situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just have a look. I'll check during the break whether your quote appears in what is now P739 which seems very much the same as I had already under tab 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour my quotation, I remember it, was on the second -- the third full paragraph. It ended with a sentence those departing will not be allowed to return.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I say, Your Honour, I don't have these documents in front of me but I had cause during yesterday's hearing to have 739 sent through to me from my office, and it was identical to the document that was in the bundle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but, no, the question is whether the quote appears there. I couldn't find it. I'll check that during the first break and not spend any time on it at this very moment. Then the marked map, of course, needs not to be, perhaps not to be admitted into evidence but it was a document which was -- the sketch, C1, was produced initially by me and marked by the witness and is in evidence now, unless there is any objection, as C1. I hear no objection. Then finally the map, the detailed map with the stadium in the left bottom corner has not been provided with a number yet. Mr. Registrar, that would be?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think the Registrar and I discussed that earlier. We worked -- I think he wasn't sure whether to give it a P number or a D number. I'm entirely neutral on the subject, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: As am I, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was provided by the Prosecution, although on the request of the claim so therefore we would give it a P number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P1035, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Then we go to the D exhibits. There we start with D115. That's the report on the work of the Bosanski Novi municipality Crisis Staff. Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The next one, D116, the photograph, three photographs, D116 A, B, and C. Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then D117 is a document related to the 1560 persons handed over to the International Committee of the Red Cross. It was marked for identification or --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: My recollection, Your Honour, is this document was shown to the witness; he could not give any indication in respect of those 1560 persons. He knew nothing about that transfer. We suggested that it be marked for identification only. Therefore we would object to its admission at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's my recollection and I'm content with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Even if marked for identification, Mr. Registrar, do we assign numbers to those documents that were marked for identification?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then the document is marked for identification and the Registrar will further inform us about numbering of those documents that were marked for identification. Having dealt with this, there is one issue I would like to see whether we can settle that right away, Mr. Josse, and that is the document which could not be translated because it was illegible. That was -- let me just see. I think it was D116.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: 114, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, 106, D106. Again very helpfully the Registrar showed it to me earlier and I asked him to have it available for Your Honours to see. I understand the position that we sent it back to the CLSS and asked them to translate those parts that they were able to translate and they've been unable to assist at this stage. In our submission, the Court should invite the CLSS to translate those parts that are legible. Most of the document appears reasonably legible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I suggest the following approach? Both parties are assisted by persons who speak and read B/C/S. Could those who are assisting the parties advise counsel on whether they could agree on the legible portions of this text? Because it seems to me that quite some of the text is legible. I fully accept and I fully appreciate the caution taken by the -- by CLSS. At the same time it appears to me that there should be a solution for at least 80, if not 90 or 95 per cent of the text. Would the parties see whether they could agree on what is legible and what the text says? And perhaps for those purposes, create a text showing what they understand the original to present?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And then send that to the CLSS?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then to send that to the CLSS and see whether the CLSS on the basis of this agreement among the parties could proceed in perhaps translating the text the parties provided to CLSS so that they are not responsible any more for the right interpretation of what appears in the original. And that that's then, upon an agreement of the parties, the Chamber could consider whether or not to admit the original text and perhaps give a number to the agreed text. Because then if the text would produced in Cyrillic, then, of course, the Chamber is in a position also to see whether it can find more or less the same letters in Cyrillic in the agreed document compared to the original one so that we take the responsibility based upon an agreement between the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The Defence is certainly agreeable to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: As are we, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then the Chamber waits to give a decision and does not urge at this moment the Defence to withdraw D106. Having dealt with these documents, it might be that later on today, the Chamber will pay further attention to some pending matters such as experts, et cetera, but at this moment we would like to proceed to hear the next witness unless there is anything the parties would like to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: There is, Your Honour. There are three other items relating to the testimony of Mr. Pasic and the exhibits relating to those yesterday. Your Honour, tab 20 which was the information of the 8th of June there was an issue as to the legibility of the signature. When we recessed, I informed the Chamber that I would attempt to get a more legible copy. We endeavoured to do that. We have a slightly more legible copy which we can supply to the Registrar and will do so today. In respect of Prosecution Exhibit 1030 which was a handwritten list of names omitting three words at the top which was read into the record, what those words were, we now have a new translation and we will supply the Chamber with, that retranslation including the three words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From what was said yesterday, Mr. Harmon, it did not give me the impression that it was an attendance list but, rather, the text suggested something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well recognition whatever it is, Your Honour, I think the record should be complete and the document as part of the evidence should have that proper translation in it. There the is the issue of contextual documents. I'm not sure when the Chamber wants to raise that issue. I only have one contextual document I wanted to submit to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would that one be a contextual document not appearing on the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It would appear on the list. It's tab 31, Your Honour, that's an overview of data of the ethnic composition of the municipalities from 1991 to 1995. It was prepared by the Ministry of Internal Affairs, and it reflects the ethnic data of Muslim, Serbs, Croats in the municipality both in 1991 and 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And -- that's comparative. It's not the -- it's not the census results.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No. This was a document prepared by the Ministry of Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then Mr. Josse --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have a copy of it. I can show it to Mr. Josse at some point in time when I'm absent, Mr. Tieger can come to a resolution on that but that's what it is. And there is one final matter, Your Honour, and that is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So Mr. Josse, we'll hear from you within one or two days whether there is any objection. It seems to be a very --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd like to think -- one further look at it bearing in mind the opportunity has been -- the offer has been made. I very much doubt whether I'll object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. How much time would you need.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I actually would happily do it at the next break and respond immediately thereafter, so long as Mr. Tieger is prepared to remain in court and show me the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I suggested one or two days so that would do, within two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The final matter, Your Honour, is during the course of the testimony of Mr. Pasic in December, I'm referring to the transcript at page 19700. Referring to lines 7 through 9, Mr. Pasic had been asked a number of questions about what proceedings had happened in courts in the municipality of Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was about judgements given by the Bosanski Novi court.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the Banja Luka court as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have any further information about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, at page 19700 it said the Court was interested in receiving information. I do have additional information about that. The question I have is the form of the submission because two things I'd like to inform the Chamber of. One, we prepared a mission, considerable time ago, I think possibly even before this trial started. It may have been during the course of this trial, but in any event there were contacts made with the judge in that municipality. We asked that judge to provide us with all files of a particular nature. Our staff members went to review those files and we have the conclusions of that. In addition to that, once Your Honour had raised the issue that you were interested I recontacted people in our office, our field office, and they have made contact with the Court once again and we will have additional information that we need to -- that I don't have at hand because it's only now being collected. But I'm prepared to submit that both to the Defence and to Your Honours, specifically as well in relation to the one case that was mentioned by Mr. Pasic dealing with the killing of a Muslim by -- I think his name was Husein Hotic so we have that data or I expect to receive that data and I'm prepared to submit that to the Chamber but the question is in what form. I'm prepared to submit it likewise to my colleagues from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you have the material available I take it, of course, I do not know whether it's exculpatory yes or no but at least if you since the Chamber asked for it that you should disclose it to the Defence. If Prosecution and Defence could reach an agreement on how to present that material, not whether to present that material but how to present that material, because the Chamber has shown an interest in receiving it. So therefore, if it would not come, we might even order one of the parties to produce that material. But if you could find a way of how to introduce it and agree on that, the Chamber would like to know. If not, then the Chamber, of course, depending on the -- of the kind of material, is it a report drafted by a person which could testify or is it just records of court proceedings, are these complete records, are they incomplete records, depending on the content of the material the Chamber will then give you guidance as to how to introduce that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's helpful, Your Honour. Thank you. We'll consult on that and if I could have this document which is tab 31, the census or the material on ethnic structure of the municipality passed to Mr. Josse, then he can examine it and give Mr. Tieger his response and if he could return that copy to me I would appreciate it because it's my records. Thank you very much, Your Honour, and if I may be excused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, are you ready to call your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No protective measures required?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would be Mr. Kapetina.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Kapetina, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Kapetina, yes. Madam Usher, would you please escort the witness into the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Kapetina, I presume.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kapetina, before giving evidence, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. May I invite you to make that declaration, of which the text has already been handed out to you by Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kapetina. Please be seated. Mr. Kapetina, you'll first be examined by Mr. Josse, counsel for the Defence. Mr. Josse, you may proceed. Examined by Mr. Josse:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're Dragan Kapetina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A leading question, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't know if anyone else is experiencing that difficulty but I'm getting some fairly oppressive feedback.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Ditto.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that seems to be what we used to call the Mexican dog, I think, which means circular sound. Is there anything which is open which should not be open? Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you a series of leading questions, if I may, Mr. Kapetina, dealing with your background. You studied politics at university; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: That's right. I studied in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were a member of the League of Communists?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: Yes. I was a member of the League of Communists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we need the assistance of the technicians because whoever speaks there seems to be a problem, and it distracts our attention from what we -- do we need a break for the technicians to look into the matter or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kapetina, I should explain to you that this is the first day this newly renovated courtroom is used and we are facing some technical problems. If they cannot be resolved right away, we'll have the first break. We are facing the same problem. Is it just a matter of two microphones? That's a possibility. Could we create a situation in which only one microphone is open in the whole of the courtroom? I have mine open. If everyone closes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No, because -- I suppose it's just about possible to have the advocate and his -- turn his or her microphone on or off, so it's possible, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it wasn't -- it was one of the earphones which then sent the signal back into one of the microphones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think that's all right, now, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we have a -- we can proceed with this. There is no whistling any more, it seems. Mr. Josse. Mr. Kapetina, I apologise for it but that's what happens in a high-tech environment. Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you graduated, you got a scholarship with a building firm known as GP Bosna in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: Yes. While I was studying I had a scholarship from the Bosna firm in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what you did for them was effectively organised their defence obligations? Would that be a fair summary?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: Yes. I worked in the civil engineering firm of Bosna and worked in total national defence, that is to say the preparation of that company for defence purposes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then in 1984 to 1985, you got a job with the republic Secretariat for National Defence in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: Yes. I responded to an advertisement, a competition, and was taken in at the republican Secretariat for National Defence in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were promoted in 1990, just before the multi-party elections, to the job of chief inspector of the republic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: Yes. That's right. In 1990, I was appointed by the executive council of Bosnia-Herzegovina as the chief inspector for national defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And that was before the multi-party elections took place in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The evidence you're about to give will focus on the two or three years after you had taken on that job, but at some point in time, in 1992, the Court will hear that you took a job in the newly created Ministry of Defence of the Republika Srpska in Pale.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. From May 1992, I worked on professional matters within the defence Ministry of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina at Pale or rather Mount Jahorina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you in fact became Deputy Minister of defence after Dayton?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: That's right. In 1997 the government of Republika Srpska appointed me Deputy Minister of defence of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1998, you got a job where you were involved in mine removal?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: Yes. In 1998, I established a non-governmental organisation for doing away with mines and explosives and it had its headquarters in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in the year 2000 you got your present job which was working for the council for the Presidency where you were an adviser in relation to defence matters?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. As of 2001 to the present day, I have been working as an adviser for defence and security, a member of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina from Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to go back, if I may, then, to the job that you took as chief inspector, but before I do that, it might just be worth mentioning the 1990 elections. Did you stand in those elections as a candidate?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: Yes. I did take part in those elections, in 1990, at a local level, at a level of the Hadzici municipality and I was on the list of candidates for the Social Democratic Party for the local parliament, that is a party which was the legal follower of the League of Communists. And, of course, the party fared ill at the elections in Hadzici. I did not make the local parliament.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As I said a moment ago, let's turn to your professional life, and this job as chief inspector of the republic. Please tell the Court what that job involved.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: In conformity with the law, pertaining to total national defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina and pursuant to the rules of the republican Secretariat for national defence, later on the Ministry of Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I as the chief inspector in the republic had the duty of implementing supervision over the implementation of the federal law and total national defence and supervision over the implementation of the republican law on total national defence, as well as the federal law on responsibilities with respect to military service and supervision over the implementation of all bills and by-laws enacted on the basis of the three laws mentioned above. In addition to that, I -- it was my duty to perform inspection and supervision of defence preparations in the civilian structures of society in Bosnia-Herzegovina and this meant to all intents and purposes supervision over the plans of development for defence as well as the defence plans themselves and plans for extraordinary situations. To make this clearer to the Court, this meant that the civilian organisations in Bosnia-Herzegovina for planning were the republican organs, municipal organs, enterprises and other legal persons, as well as sociopolitical organisations in local communities. Of course, I should like to remind the Court that I was not authorised to perform supervision over combat readiness and the situation in units belonging to the Yugoslav People's Army and Territorial Defence. This was done by inspectors at the level of the federal state.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you retain this job after the multi-party elections?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: I continued working as the chief republican inspector, continuously from 1991, although I wasn't appointed to that most by the government of the republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. However, I should like to stress that the government did not appoint anybody to that post so I continued to work on those jobs. Of course, I waited for my appointment to the function or to be relieved of my duties. The republican inspectors do their work according to an annual programme prepared by the chief inspector and okayed by the Defence Minister. And in January I myself prepared a programme for inspection supervision relating to 1991 and I did not receive permission to work towards the implementation of that programme. I didn't know the reasons for that. So I prepared a second version of the programme for that same year, which I handed over in February. I did not receive an answer once again, nor was the okay given to the programme by the Minister of Defence and as time was running out, I was forced to prepare a third programme which I handed over in the month of March. On the basis of that third programme, I was going to implement supervision at the level of the republic. I'd like to tell the court that I wasn't the sole person in charge -- the sole person appointed to perform supervision. I was in charge of the whole business but 10 to 12 inspectors are involved in the whole process from the various ministries and organs of administration of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina who took part with me in the job of supervision and they are all authorised inspectors just like I was myself. So much for me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's briefly examine who were the leading personnel in the ministry after the elections. The Defence Minister was a man called Jerko Doko; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. The minister was the Defence was Jerko Doko, a candidate and member of the Croatian democratic community, HDZ.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the name of his deputy, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: His deputy was Hasim Begovic and he was a candidate or rather he was appointed to that post by the Party of Democratic Action, and before that post he was a professional officer, he was a colonel, in fact, of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you have already described in the answer you gave a moment ago, the difficulties you had in carrying out your job. Who did you put those difficulties down to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: Well, I did not complete my answer and inform the Court about the annual programme for inspection and supervision. Anyway, after the version I handed over in March I was called by Minister Doko to his offices to his cabinet, and I responded to that invitation and went to see him. And he told me that he had seen the earlier versions prepared by me but, of course, he didn't read through any of those versions. And then he told me in friendly terms he said, "I cannot allow you to work on matters of inspection supervision in the republic for the simple -- for a very simple reason, because then I wouldn't have completed the task and job that I had come to the ministry to do." I said to him, "Well, don't we have the same goals in the ministry, the two of us?" And that was to further the programme of the Ministry of Defence in conformity with the law. And to that, he said that they were not the priorities of the Defence Ministry and that he could not allow me to implement the programme for inspection, supervision, that he wasn't going to sign the programme but that he could assign other tasks to me which I could be involved in, and that I should forget inspection and supervision and the programmes that I had prepared. Of coarse I wanted to know what these other tasks and jobs were because it was a matter of my own job and the work that I had to do. He said that these would not be constant tasks but would be ad hoc tasks from one case to the next, and then I asked him what my first job and task would be, and he said, "Well, let's look at the specifics. You see the women that are protesting at the moment because the recruits are being sent to do their military service. They keep up their demonstrations in front of the building, in front of the executive council building and assembly, but in that group of women, we have some women who are Bosniak, who are Muslims and are Croats but there is not a single Serbian among them. So your task would be to rally four or five Serb women to help them, to write them an appropriate speech, and to have them join in with the other women, to write some slogans for them. So that would be a start. And we would pay you for that separately, of course." Without thinking, I said that any further -- I said I didn't want to do that kind of work because I didn't get my rating in the Ministry of Bosnia-Herzegovina to do work like that, and he said, "Right, fine. Then we've finished our conversation." Then he phoned up the vice premier of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Miodrag Simovic, and then he said to me, "As of today, Dragan Kapetina will no longer be engaged in the Ministry of Defence and he can be placed at your disposal, Mr. Vice Premier, if you need him." The vice premier, of course, asked me to come and see him because he didn't know what was going on. He didn't know of my conversation with Mr. Doko. So after talking to Doko, I went to the offices of vice-president Simovic and told him all about what had happened, and he said, "Well, that's how things stand. I can do nothing about that. You can expect no protection from the government. You must come to terms with what has happened and we'll see what we are going to do in future." And that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So let's be clear about this. Were you able to carry out any inspections at all?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: Well, I had to compile a programme and implement some inspection and I did have all the conditions to do that, inspection and supervision are important functions of a defence ministry because through inspection you gain an insight into the state of affairs with respect to the preparation of plans and implementation of laws both in the republic and the municipalities. So it was my duty to file a report to the government every year, the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, on the work I had done in inspection and supervision. So I had to insist that a programme be enacted and supervision and inspection be performed regardless of the situation that prevailed in Bosnia-Herzegovina because at the end of the year, as I say, I had to report to the government on the situation with respect to preparing the republic's defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, going back to the answer you gave a moment ago --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, could you invite the witness to answer your last question? Because although he spent ten lines he didn't say whether he was able to carry out any inspections. Did you finally carry out any inspections, yes or no? That's what was asked.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. At the beginning of 1991, all the conditions were in place for inspection to go ahead and even become intensified in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And were they carried out, these inspections?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those inspections were supposed to be carried out in the municipalities at that time, and in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time there were 109 municipalities including the city of Sarajevo, and, of course, the inspections were to be held at the republican level and republican organisation level, and in enterprises of special importance to the republic and its defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Now you, for the third time, told us whether the conditions were fine, what should have been done, but the question was whether these inspections were ever carried out at whatever level. If you first start saying that they were carried out and you can explain or if not, then there is no need for further explanation. Or at least --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the previous year, that is to say 1990, in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, inspection was carried out in 30 municipalities. Supervision. And it was planned that every year in the republic, inspection and supervision should be carried out in at least 30 municipalities so that during a four-year term of office, inspections will have been carried out through the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in all its municipalities. And in my programme for 1991 I adopted the is a same methods, planning at least inspections in at least 30 municipalities and I'd like to mention once again we saw the need to hold inspections because in 1990 there were some amendments to the law on defence in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kapetina, no one asked you about the usefulness, the necessity, et cetera. The simple thing we would like to know is, and you told us for 1990, 30 -- in 30 municipalities the inspection was carried out. 1991, how many?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not in a single municipality did inspections take place. I did not implement the programme at all because I didn't get the go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We didn't ask for the reasons at this moment. If we are interested to know, or if Mr. Josse is interested, he'll ask you. So we spend approximately four to five minutes now on a very simple question: Were these inspections carried out? Your answer is in 1990, still 30 inspections were carried out, whereas for 1991, no inspection was carried out. Quite simple. Just facts. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A few minutes ago, you were telling us about the difficulties that you were facing from Mr. Doko. Why do you think Mr. Doko was being so obstructive?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: At the beginning, I didn't know why he was obstructing me in performing my regular duties and tasks. However, in talking to my colleagues, assistant Defence Ministers, specifically the assistant who was appointed on behalf of the HDZ, Croatian democratic community, whom I complained to and said that I was not being allowed to do my job by the minister, he told me -- well, I asked him whether he had knowledge of any other plan being implemented at the level of the defence ministry, and he said that minister Doko had been given the task of destroying the units of the Yugoslav People's Army on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina; to all intents and purposes, to break them up. And that of the -- and to make of the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina a separate armed force of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Of course, I asked him if that was what was being done, then where are the Serbs in all this? And where is my place in all this? And as he was a good friend of mine, he said, "Well, in a situation of this kind, in the kind of situation that we have in the ministry today, you are being treated as a member of the blues." And the blue colour was assigned to the enemy at that particular time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as things became clearer what did it seem to you was the aim, the ultimate aim, of the minister?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: Well, later on, I came to the same conclusions, the same I heard from my colleague the assistant minister, that that was in fact the goal, the minister's goal, and not only the minister's goal but that was in fact the overall goal of the coalition that was being formed at the level of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is to say a coalition between the Muslim or rather the Muslim-Croat coalition, the coalition between the HDZ and the SDA parties. And as time went on, I saw that concrete steps were being taken along those lines, and that problems were being created and conflicts with the Yugoslav People's Army, the children or recruits were not being sent to the JNA to do their military service, for example, that was one of the steps, and that conflicts were being forged in places in Bosnia-Herzegovina between the population and the JNA and the employees of the Bosnia-Herzegovina ministries who were former JNAs were placed at the disposal of the JNA or the republican TO staff or, rather, I had knowledge that there was a project being worked on to create an armed force of Bosnia-Herzegovina out of the existing Territorial Defence forces but without the members of Serb ethnicity, without the Serbs taking part in that Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in 1991, towards the middle of the year, you really decided to go public on some of the difficulties that you were facing within the ministry; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Having held consultations with the vice premier, Miodrag Simovic, I decided to send a written caution to the top-most state organs saying this they were behaving unlawfully and unconstitutionally, and those organs were first and foremost the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which numbered seven members of the time, then the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I sent them written warnings telling them that they weren't working in conformity with the federal and republican laws and that they were taking authorisations upon themselves that were legitimately given over to other organisations and organs and I told them without mincing words who was violating federal laws. So this warning of mine was not accepted by them or was not met by them in the way I had in mind, the way they should have taken this on board because the government did not --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just pause. Let's deal with the reaction to these letters in one moment's time. Let's deal with the appeal or the letters that you wrote. Before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, before doing so, could the witness clarify the ethnicity of Mr. Simovic, that's still unclear to me whereas the --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us whether he was a Croat, a Muslim, a Serb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Miodrag Simovic was the vice Prime Minister, and he was appointed on behalf of the Serbian democratic party which means that he is a Serb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just say, if you will allow me, Mr. Simovic was a particularly in charge of defence, the internal affairs and general administration in the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that is why I was told to report to him and to consult with him. That's what I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the letter that you wrote, did anyone ask you to write it? Did you come under any pressure to write it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: Nobody forced me or talked me into writing this letter. I simply concluded that I might end up having problems if I didn't inform the highest republican organs that there was no inspection in the republic. If I had waited until the end of the year I should have submitted my report then and I was in no position to submit any reports because that report would have been a blank piece of paper. That's why I decided to write this warning letter and I only consulted with Mr. Simovic, the vice premier, in order to see whether I would face any consequences if I did that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, to the best of your knowledge, there are no copies still in existence of this letter, is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: I did not see a copy of that letter. That letter stayed in my office. Of course, it should have ended up in the Presidency, in the government, but I believe that the media in Bosnia-Herzegovina published parts of that letter of mine - I'm talking about the written media - and they were also conveyed by the television, but not in prime time, but in the first news programme between 1800 and 1900 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could the witness be given the Defence Exhibit bundle, please, and could everyone turn to tab 5? Yes, I'm trying to get into better habits here, could I ask for an exhibit number straight away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 5, Your Honours, will be D118.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if we look, Mr. Kapetina, at the original B/C/S version, we see in the top right-hand corner an article and we see in Latin script your name, Dragan Kapetina, don't we?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just tell us about this publication. We see that at the bottom right-hand corner. What's this newspaper called?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: This was published in a paper called Narodna Armija, people's army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did this -- where was this newspaper published, in what part of the country?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: I believe that Narodna Armija was published in Belgrade. Prior to that I had not seen this text but I know that the printed media in Sarajevo also published parts of my warning letter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which -- just dealing with that, which Bosnian newspapers are you aware of your letter being reported in?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, this was published in Oslobodjenje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Now, what -- it's a small extract. It's quite important so I am going to ask you to read through this, please. Read the whole article, including the heading of the article, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, this is just an author's remark and the title is "encouraging lawlessness." And the text reads the decision of the BiH government that delays the application of the law and changes in amendment to the law on military service and law on changes and amendments to the law on all people's Defence in the territory of BH are unconstitutional and illegal because the BH government does not have the competency to declare null and void and to delay the application of federal laws and other regulations passed by the competent organs. It is in the exclusive competence of the SFRY assembly which passed them to declare null and void or to delay the application of the aforementioned to federal laws. The decision of the BiH government which demands that military service and mobilisation in the republic be carried out in the same manner as before, that is in a manner not legally regulated, until further notice, is also legal. By this the government directly encourages lawlessness and anarchy in the field of military service and mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, before we continue, it appears to me looking at the original that this is a part of a larger publication, with two additions to it in these frames. So therefore by just translating this portion we miss the context in which Mr. Kapetina is quoted in this article. Have you considered the remainder -- first of all, is my impression right? Or.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let -- may I deal with it this way initially?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kapetina, you -- have you had a chance to look at everything that is written on the piece of paper in front of you? In other words, the newspaper article that is -- that dominates the page that you have in front of you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I have not read it before I saw it here, and I cannot comment upon the entire text that has been published on this page. However, the essence of this text and what the author wanted to say is that the Presidency and the government do one thing, and the chief republican inspector warns them that what they do is not in keeping with the law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just try and answer my question. His is an example of why it's important to try and answer the question. If you didn't understand it then I apologise. The question was: I know that you've been given this piece of paper in advance of your coming into the witness box, correct? This piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: Excuse me, what is your question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps if you would look at me for a moment. Have you read the article that I am pointing to at the moment? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: I repeat: I actually read the second part of the text here when I was preparing for this testimony. I had not seen this text from Narodna Armija before. However, I realise that in addition to the fact that the Presidency and the government did things unlawfully, they had not respected the agreements that I had reached with the federal organs. It says here that there was an agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kapetina, may I again ask you to answer to the question? The question was whether you had read the article Mr. Josse was pointing at that was the whole of the page. Then you said I actually read the second part of the text. So your answer is partially yes. And no one yet asked you to explain to us what you realised, I don't know on the basis of what, but you seem to have realised something. And please focus on the questions, answer them, and then whatever additional information is needed, Mr. Josse will certainly ask you for it. Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kapetina, as I've already said, I am aware that you were given this piece of paper a few days ago when you arrived in The Hague. And, of course, you have read the passage in the top right-hand corner that contains your name. What we are interested in is the rest of this page. Have you read the article that forms the bulk of this page, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: I've read the entire article but I'm not in a position to analyse it thoroughly and to draw up its concept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kapetina, no one asked you to analyse. If Mr. Josse will ask you, you just say, "I can't do that." Wait until the next question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My second question was not going to be whether you can analyse it but whether you can summarise it. If the answer is no, say so.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA
utterances.text: I'm not in a position to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, the Defence is invited to provide a full translation because there seems to be some relation, the name "Doko" appears often. It seems from at first sight --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It will be submitted beyond a shadow of a doubt. I should say as is clear from -- this isn't a criticism. It's quite the opposite. As is clear from the English translation, the translation that the Court has was provided to the Defence by the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And I'm grateful to them for disclosing it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to move on to an intercept next. I don't know -- again, I'm reliant on my learned friend and his assistant.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't know what time the Court intends to break but if we are moving to an intercept this might be an appropriate time to do so and then we can have it set up when we resume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, we are now on our way. If we would have a break now could we play the intercept afterwards?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That would be convenient. If it can't be set up we'll deal with it by the way of transcript. If it can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but I take it that it must be possible in this new, hi-tech environment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm advised that -- I leave it to the Court and to Mr. Josse, of course, but I should at least tell the Court it could be played immediately if anyone so desired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How long is the --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm afraid I've only read it. I've never listened to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It can be played after the break without any problem. Then the witness has freshly in his mind what he heard and can answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think that would be preferable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We will adjourn until ten minutes past four.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, before I give you an opportunity to continue the examination of the witness, I'd like to deal with a few more procedural matters. The first thing I'd like to do is to say a few more words about the Davidovic issue, because the Chamber would like to draw attention to this issue that arose last summer during the cross-examination of Mr. Davidovic, a witness who was called by the Prosecution. During his cross-examination, Mr. Davidovic was accused of being a liar and a criminal. A number of specific criminal allegations were made against him by the Defence while no corroborating evidence was produced in support. This prompted a discussion between the parties regarding the acceptability of this line of questioning. On the 15th of December 2005, the Chamber filed its written decision on this matter. The Chamber attaches great importance to the dissemination of this decision, bearing in mind that the way the cross-examination was conducted could have a deterrent effect on future witnesses. The Chamber is aware that although the decision is filed publicly, not all members of the public have easy access to the written decisions of the Tribunal. The Chamber therefore has decided to briefly summarise the content of the decision in open court, so this does not replace the decision but it's just a brief non-authoritative summary in order to draw the attention of the public to the decision. The Chamber finds that the Defence has the right to ask a witness pointed questions, even if this process may be an unpleasant experience for the witness. However, the questions must be fair. When a party wishes to confront a witness with what effectively constitutes allegations that the witness has engaged in serious criminal conduct, that party must have reasonable grounds to do so at the time the allegations are made. Reasonable grounds does not require that the party has in its possession incontrovertible evidence of wrongdoing. It does, however, require that they base their accusation on something more than a mere hunch, innuendo, or on unsubstantiated hearsay. Strong language may be acceptable in cross-examination, given that the party has a solid basis for making their allegations that a witness has engaged in criminal activities. Accordingly, the weaker the party's grounds for making such an allegation the more caution is called for on behalf of the cross-examining counsel. In the case of Mr. Davidovic, the Chamber concluded that the Defence had not demonstrated reasonable grounds to formulate the allegations in the manner they did and that therefore the Chamber regrets the Defence's use of these inappropriate phrases. This concludes this summary of the written and already-filed decision in relation to Mr. Davidovic. Then, Mr. Tieger, this is not primarily your problem but could be that of Mr. Harmon. I asked him about tab 17. He then told us that tab 17 actually was -- I think it was P793 but let me just check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I reread the transcript and the exhibit was introduced on page 19777 and a quote was given from that exhibit on the next pages. I told Mr. Harmon that I could not find the quote in tab 17, and Mr. Harmon then said, it should be a document, 1st Krajina Corps dated the 1st, June the 1st, in tab 17. I told him that I had got a document under tab 17 of the 9th of June and I think today Mr. Harmon provided us again with that same document of the 9th of June, which from what I see does not contain the quote. I asked the Registrar to provide me with -- I think Mr. Harmon provided us with 739. That's again the 9th of June, without the quote he gave. So therefore the puzzle is not solved. And I now check in the original 739 and that's exactly what we find under tab 17. It does not contain the quote and is not a document of the 1st of June where Mr. Harmon indicated he was quoting from a document dated the 1st of June. So providing us again with the same document, which does not contain the quote he gave, does not resolve the matter. Would you please pass this message to Mr. Harmon and then we'll hear from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then next procedural issue. Quite a number of translations have been provided by both parties since already some time. Have the parties checked whether, on the basis of these translations, there are any further objections against admission for these documents which are provisionally admitted and waiting for translation? And I'll just mention them. That's D75, D78, D80, D82H, D82I, D83, D90 to and including 98, D99A to D99V, including the last one. D101 to 105, D107, D108, D110, and D111. I checked that they all appear correctly on the transcript. Now, any objection in relation to these documents or would you need more time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If the Court would grant some limited additional time it would permit me the opportunity to check with everyone who might have been involved with those particular exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two days would do?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I believe so, Your Honour thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then same question for you, Mr. Josse, in relation to P967, P974, P986 to P991, the latter included, and P993 to 1007, the latter included.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, two days, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two days. We'll hear from you in two days. Then a few more matters. First of all, expert witnesses. The deadline was set at 13th of January. We have received indication of the subject matter of two expert reports that the Chamber can expect to be presented. We have not yet received any names of experts. Nevertheless, also for the Prosecution to prepare, the Chamber suggests that if you would not have invited the experts to write a report, and they should be presented by the 28th of February, that they hardly have any time to write it any more. So therefore the Chamber urges the defence to indicate that they have invited the experts and which experts to prepare these reports. Mr. Josse, could you say anything about the selection of the experts?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, if I've been frank with the Court I'd much rather say absolutely nothing at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's media and military.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, one primary reason and that's that Mr. Stewart is dealing with this. If the Court wishes to hear from him in relation to this matter, perhaps the Court would set a day later this week for him to come and address Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but we have a deadline for the presentation of the reports, at the 28th of February. It goes without saying it's of no use to invite an expert to write a report on the 25th if the report has to be presented on the 28th. Therefore, there should be for preparation, and the Chamber suggests at this moment that the Defence should give the names of those experts, well, let's say, within a week from now on, even if the reports, of course, will not be ready by then but we at least, and especially also the Prosecution, knows what to expect.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm certainly not going to argue with that proposition. I simply invite the Court to say that if Mr. Stewart wishes to develop the matter any further, he's at liberty to come to this Court when it's sitting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And subject to a little bit of notice to a legal officer and the Prosecution, address the Court further on the subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As it stands now the Chamber would like to receive -- to know that the names of the experts are disclosed to the Prosecution within the next seven days. Let's be quite clear. Of course, there could be a reason to come and argue the matter in court, but the Chamber would prefer if the time is spent on selecting the experts rather than to argue why no time could have been found to select an expert. I think that's clear enough. Because the Chamber is concerned about the presentation of the reports because the longer it takes to select your experts the bigger the chance that the presentation of the -- that the filing of the reports will not be done as expected.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm not seeking to be disrespectful. I understand what Your Honour is saying. There is nothing I can honestly and usefully add at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Josse, for not adding anything. Then another matter is the Chamber has been provided with the names of two new witnesses who did not appear yet on the list of witnesses that the Chamber is in possession of. I'm fully aware, and the Chamber is fully aware that this list might not be the final one, to say the least. At the same time, of course, the Chamber would have preferred to have a revised list already and the Chamber understands that the Defence is working hard on this revised list. Nevertheless, if you want to add a witness which is not yet on the list and it was a relatively long list, then this should be approved by the Chamber. I'm fully aware of the present situation in which working on the basis of a list which is not a very realistic one doesn't make that much sense. At the same time, the Chamber reminds the Defence of what the Rules require and urges the Defence to finalise its revised list as soon as possible so that we have again a realistic basis to work on, and that brings me to another matter. The Chamber was notified in the -- well, I would say in the -- was notified the testimony of Mr. Krajisnik would start on the 23rd of January. It now seems that other witnesses are put on the list to testify soon so therefore the Chamber would not be surprised if Mr. Krajisnik would not start his testimony on the 23rd of January. At the same time, it reminds us of the very unpractical situation which exists at this moment that there is no schedule whatsoever and new witnesses are put in without the consent of the Chamber. The Chamber wants to hear from the Defence a bit more about their plans because finally, and that's the same issue that I raised in respect of the experts, everything is postponed and at a certain moment there is no time left and the Chamber can imagine that then one would say, but you couldn't deny this, you couldn't deny that. We were left without any guidance as to how the Defence wanted, without any realistic guidance as to how the Defence wanted to present its case. The Chamber then decided to grant some additional time and so we do not know anything and, later on, there will be no possibility to refer to changing circumstances because there is not even a beginning. So we can't compare the situation as it was when we took the decision to grant, I think it was an additional seven weeks, in the present situation. The Chamber is very concerned about postponing, whether it's experts, whether it's putting in new witnesses, whether it's postponing the testimony of Mr. Krajisnik, and the Chamber does not want to be misunderstood. That is, when it gave its earlier decision on how much time was available, that it was firm in its determination. If there is anything to be added Mr. Josse, you have an opportunity to do so but it's rather an outcry of the Chamber that it would rather work on a realistic and practical basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, all the matters that Your Honour has just raised are of extreme importance to everyone concerned with this trial. They are matters that are primarily being dealt with by my leader, and really he needs to address the Chamber upon them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It won't surprise the court to know that I could deal with each of these matters in turn. Some I have rather more responsibility for than others. However, I'm firmly of the view that the desirable course will be for Mr. Stewart to read Your Honour's words which have just been transcribed, to consider the matter, and either in writing or perhaps orally to come back in the next few days and set out what the exact position is. If the Court is satisfied with that, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm not expecting --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It would be extremely desirable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do not expect you to respond extensively on the matter, Mr. Josse. I think the message should be heard clearly and loudly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: He will certainly have Your Honour's words relayed to him in a clear and indeed loud fashion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand that you can't hear loudly but you can hear loud words and you can hear clear words so I apologise for not linguistically being correct. That's -- these were the procedural issues I would like to raise at this moment. Mr. Harmon, I see you reappeared. I don't know whether it's for tab 17 which is always on my mind, as you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I noticed Your Honour, I noticed it on the television and it stimulated me to come down here. I thought I would try to resolve that matter and we discussed that while I was here, and I will -- I need to further attempt to resolve that because what is the document that Your Honours have clearly does not have the quotation that I quoted. It may be that 739 is the wrong exhibit number. I'm going to go back to my office and e-mail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will hear and understand everything after you've given your explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. If I may be excused ones again, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are. It was not even necessary for you to come down here specifically for --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I did not want to leave Mr. Tieger abandoned on that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then the witness can be brought back into the courtroom again so that you, Mr. Josse, can continue your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Josse: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kapetina, I'm sorry that you had to wait for some time because I had to deal with some procedural issues. Mr. Josse will continue his examination. Would you please be so kind carefully listen to what he asks you and to specifically answer to those questions. Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just before we hear the intercept --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise but I wasn't receiving the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll have to check whether you're on the right channel. Did you miss everything I said? Because then I'll repeat it, Mr. Kapetina. I first apologised that you had to wait for such a long time because we had to deal with procedural issues. Mr. Josse will continue his examination and I urged you to listen carefully to what he asks so that you specifically answer his question and wait for any further details whether they are needed yes or no. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what I said was just before we turn to the intercept, we have seen an extract from your letter, from a -- contained within a newspaper, the article being dated the 18th of September 1991. Do you remember when you wrote the letter, when you sent it to the government?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly. I don't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could we all now turn to tab 4, please? And I'd like you to listen, if you would, Mr. Kapetina, to the following intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I presume no one else is receiving any audio. What I can tell the Court is I can see the synchronised version running in the screen in the fashion that it normally does when we heard it consistently in the past. I don't know if this is another glitch of this particular courtroom in its newly renovated state or if it's something we can remedy --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I noticed that we do not receive any spoken English translation. We do, however, receive on the French channel, a French translation. But for the completeness of the transcript --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters would like a reference because they weren't able to find the section as it did not start from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I can imagine that that's the problem. Perhaps part of it was lost, it seems, but please correct me if I'm wrong, Mr. Josse, the name of Kapetina appeared quite quickly in B/C/S, and I do see that the second part of page 1 of the four pages contains the name of Kapetina.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, I was told almost immediately by Mrs. Slavajevic [phoen] that the point that we picked it up was towards the bottom of page 1 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We have located it, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then could we restart the audio?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "Radovan KARADZIC: Yes. "Vule DIVLJAN: Hello. "Radovan KARADZIC: Yes. "Vule DIVLJAN: Radovan. "Radovan KARADZIC: Yes. "Vule DIVLJAN: It's Vule Divljan. How are you? "Radovan KARADZIC: Hey, Vule, hi. What's up? "Vule DIVLJAN: What are you up to? "Radovan KARADZIC: I've got a lot to do. "Vule DIVLJAN: Look. We should call a few people together as soon as possible relating to national defence. I'm here with the chief inspector and the situation is alarming. "Radovan KARADZIC: In what sense? "Vule DIVLJAN: Well, there is fucking chaos. They should inform you about everything, about how things are going, what's being done, et cetera. For example, some people were invited to the council session yesterday to support some horrible things and so on. "Radovan KARADZIC: Okay. Is Simovic informed about this? "Vule DIVLJAN: Well, I don't know but if he is he should have informed you right away about what is to be done. "Radovan KARADZIC: All right we know mainly about what's being done but do ... what Doko and the associates are doing isn't worth a hill of beans. The army is there too ... at that. Well have a council meeting tonight, issue a declaration supporting the motions the army has taken to guard the country and endorsing the mobilisation. Therefore ... "Vule DIVLJAN: Could Dragan Kapetina, the chief inspector come to this council session and provide additional information as to what this is all about because he knows about everything that's being done. And it's true, I don't know what he can do. "Radovan KARADZIC: Dragan Kapetina? "Vule DIVLJAN: Yes. "Radovan KARADZIC: And how does he see all this and how things are going? Put him on. "Vule DIVLJAN: Just a moment. "Dragan KAPETINA: Yes. Hello? "Radovan KARADZIC: Yes. "Dragan KAPETINA: May I help you? How are you? This is chief inspector for national defence. "Radovan KARADZIC: Well, tell me, please, what can you tell me about that. "Dragan KAPETINA: Well, I can tell you about the implementation of the ministry's function. "Radovan KARADZIC: Yes. "Dragan KAPETINA: In that field? "Radovan KARADZIC: Yes. "Dragan KAPETINA: That it's not being implemented and that secondary things are being pushed through while the main function is not being implemented. There is practically a complete blockade. "Radovan KARADZIC: Who is blocking it? "Dragan KAPETINA: Well, I couldn't say. It's more or less known who is in charge of the organ and that the activities are to go from the minister. "Radovan KARADZIC: What are the duties of an inspector? "Dragan KAPETINA: Well, the duties of the inspector are mainly directed towards or rather downwards towards the opposite ... towards the municipal organs, towards everyone that's here. "Radovan KARADZIC: We know about the telegrams he sent, we know about Mesic's message. And tell me, do you have any competences other than that of the minister? Can you address anyone else officially? "Dragan KAPETINA: Well, I just told you now, I can only address the municipalities, my subjects and ... I don't know whether I can ... for example, the competences were such that charges could be pressed .... everything that ... with the law ... if it's lawfully implemented. "Radovan KARADZIC: All right. It's your opinion that things are not being done in accordance with the law in the field, right? "Dragan KAPETINA: It's my opinion that we have no instructions for the work of municipal organs. In my opinion, for example, the republic and the state are under the imminent threat of war, and we're giving no instructions or directions to the municipal organs about how to operate. And not only to them but to other subjects as well, who are obliged to carry out preparations. "Radovan KARADZIC: Why aren't you giving them any? "Dragan KAPETINA: I don't know that. I suppose that is blocked. Because we don't even have meetings or agreements or ... I don't know whether that's because a board hasn't been constituted here or why.
