I don't know if it's because of reinforcement but we are fully supplied. Whether that's ... whether that's old or new that's none of my business. "Radovan KARADZIC: I would like to ask you ... I mean, I mean ... you know very well what Doko is doing. "Dragan KAPETINA: Yes, I sort of do. "Radovan KARADZIC: So I'm asking you to write an official record, that is a report right now in your capacity as inspector to the Prime Minister ... to write a report to the minister and send the same report to the Prime Minister and the corps commander and to the TO commander. "Dragan KAPETINA: I can only address the government, my competence only covers the government. "Radovan KARADZIC: Look, please write this and send copies to the corps commander and the commander of the TO. "Dragan KAPETINA: I thought that we should ask for an urgent meeting with the minister this morning and then he could put forth the concept and we would be informed of what he's doing. "Radovan KARADZIC: You know very well what ... you know very well what Doko is doing. Every ministry knows what Doko is doing. Therefore you are, you are like subject in this entire system. It would be best if you did that. Write to the government, inform the government of this in detail and inform them about what's being done and what's not being done and is supposed to be. Inform them of things being done and should not be, as well as of things that we are obliged to do and yet are not doing. Inform the government and send a copy to the president of the BH assembly and the president of the council for national defence, Izetbegovic and the two commanders of the corps and the TO. "Dragan KAPETINA: And could you do something and arrange a meeting between myself and Simovic? Because Simovic is far more skilled in this field and has more experience. "Radovan KARADZIC: Well, call Simovic, he'll see you. I'll call him myself right now. "Dragan KAPETINA: Good. If you announce me to Simovic then Terzic, our undersecretary here and I would ... "Radovan KARADZIC: Yes. "Dragan KAPETINA: And we would agree for this active the to really be coordinated and not ... "Radovan KARADZIC: Look, two-three people from the ministry are responsible for this, including the minister. We know very well what's happening. Several people from the ministry will be responsible but who ... those for whom we know very well how much they are helping Doko in the devising of tricks against Yugoslavia and against the state and in the disruption of the defensive power of the state, instead of helping it. We know that. It's well known and it's known where it needs to be known and it's known both by political and military structures. And you should act, please, according to your conscience. Urgently. Regardless of how far your competence reaches. You have the right to ... send a copy of your report to the government, to send it to the president of the council for national defence, Izetbegovic and ... "Dragan KAPETINA: Listen. "Radovan KARADZIC: And the corps commander and the commander of the TO. But that should be done urgently today. Send it via courier. "Dragan KAPETINA: All right. "Radovan KARADZIC: Otherwise you'll be a responsible man and Pusina will be responsible and the entire ministry over there. All the people in the ministry. Because you're not small children to be waiting around for the minister. You're carrying out your function. "Dragan KAPETINA: Agreed. "Radovan KARADZIC: I'll announce to Simovic now that you'll ... "Dragan KAPETINA: Arrange a meeting with Simovic so that this ... "Radovan KARADZIC: All right, I'll call him. "Dragan KAPETINA: ... has some legal foundation after all. "Radovan KARADZIC: I'll call him now. "Dragan KAPETINA: Thank you. "Radovan KARADZIC: Cheers."

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could that have a number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D119, Your Honours. The transcript would be D119.A and the English translation D119.A.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Firstly, who is the man who is heard at the beginning of the tape, Mr. Divljan?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think Divljan worked in some other republican organ and that he came together with a colleague to see me in my office. But I don't know which organ he worked for.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are we right to assume from this intercept that at that point in time, that is the 1st of July 1991, you had not written the letter you have told us about earlier?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. I didn't write a letter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How soon after this conversation with Dr. Karadzic did you write the letter?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know exactly but within the space of seven to 10 days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To what extent were you influenced by what Dr. Karadzic was saying to you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I should first of all like to emphasise that I didn't ask to have this talk at my own initiative; neither did Dr. Karadzic, I assume. I did not -- I was not subject to anybody's influence, especially if the people wielding influence on me are not my superiors. I was completely independent in my work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, had you ever spoken to Dr. Karadzic before? If you don't know, say so.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'd never spoken to him before, either over the phone or directly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And for the avoidance of any doubt, what did you understand him being asked -- him asking you to do?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood him to be asking me that Mr. Karadzic was asking me to link up with the army command, the republican staff of Territorial Defence and quite simply to take an active part in the Ministry of Defence frameworks. Of course, I understood from our conversation that he was not fully informed of my own competences and authority as a chief republican inspector.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any idea as to how Dr. Karadzic found out what your position and viewpoint was within the ministry?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether at the time of this conversation he was aware of my positions and of my position in the ministry. I myself did not inform him about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why were you anxious to see Mr. Simovic at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to have a conversation with Mr. Simovic because the Defence Ministry is part of the government, Minister of Defence is a member of the government, and Mr. Simovic was vice premier for Defence and internal policies and he was a very experienced politician. He had spent a long time working in the state administration and I knew that he was aware and familiar with the administration. Most of the other staff who joined the state administration had never before worked in the state administration, unlike Simovic, who had even before that spent a number of years working in the state administration.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your -- I'm going to move on. Your letter is published, it's widely circulated, it gets a certain amount of publicity, both in the newspapers, as we've seen, and you tell us on the television. Is there any reaction by Mr. Doko to what -- to this publicity?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Minister Doko did not react to the publicity in the media. On the contrary, he received my caution with the invitation to attend a session of the council for state Defence because he was a member of that council, the council for state defence of the republic, and when he received this written warning, together with the other materials and agenda for the session, he called me to his office, he threw that piece of paper across the table towards me and he asked me what this was. I informed him what this was. I told him that this was my duty and my legal obligation to warn the highest state bodies about the need to respect legality, and then he asked "What law should be respected?" And then I said, "Mr. Minister, those laws and the constitution which are in force, which are being applied, both federal and the republican ones." And then he said that he did not recognise those laws and that constitution. He used very vulgar language. And we had words then and I left the office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall when that conversation was, approximately?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That conversation took place two or three days before the session of the council for National Defence that was scheduled and that I should have attended myself in order to directly warn the Presidency about that letter of warning and about what I thought.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you physically go to the building where the meeting you've just mentioned, the session, council of National Defence, was being held?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was invited by the secretary of the council, the professional who prepared those sessions. I went there. I was waiting in front of the meeting room for my item on the agenda to be called.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Expecting to be called in to deal with it presumably; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as far as you're aware, what happened?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given the fact that the Vice-Premier Miodrag Simovic was a member of the council for National Defence, when my item was called, that written warning, the president of that council, Mr. Izetbegovic, the chairman of the Presidency, asked Simovic, who was the vice-premier, because the ministry was part of the government, he asked him to inform members of the council and to tell them whether I, as the chief republican inspector was authorised to warn the highest republican organ. Miodrag Simovic informed the chair person and other members of the council that I was duty-bound to issue that warning to everybody and tell them that they were duty-bound to obey laws, and that I acted in keeping with my responsibilities and with my legal authorities. And if I hadn't done so, the government should have -- could have called me to task. After that explanation was given by the vice-premier, Mr. Izetbegovic suggested that the item should be removed from the agenda and this is exactly what was done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall when that session was held?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't. I don't remember the date when that session took place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After it, did you continue to work at the ministry?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I continued coming to work but I didn't do much. I didn't do anything. Not only me. There were a lot of people like me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you any idea why the minister allowed you to remain in your job, bearing in mind what had just transpired?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that there was no time for any showdowns or, for example, for my job to be terminated or any such radical moves. The minister at that time had more urgent things to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you about some specific events within the ministry in 1992. Did anything happen in relation to the arming of staff within the ministry?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know exactly when that happened, but I can tell you that I was informed by a lady who worked in the ministry and who was in charge with the plan of the defence of the ministry, and who kept 36 pistols in a vault, she told me that Mr. Doko asked her to give those pistols to Croats and Muslims against receipt. I don't know when this happened but I believe that it was in the summer of 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did you find this out?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned that from this lady, who was in charge of the defence plan of the ministry, and she was in charge of those pistols. Those pistols were envisaged for the staff who would have worked in the Ministry of Defence during the war, if there had been a war. And also, the assistant minister -- Defence Minister confirmed to me that they had been issued with those pistols as their personal weapon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see or hear of any other discrimination against Serbs within the ministry?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I did. Again, I can't tell you when this happened but a decree law was passed by the law on coming to work because it had already become visible that a number of Serbs in the ministry and other bodies failed to turn up for work for security reasons. And then a decree law was passed that a register should be kept of those who were coming to work and I believe that it was stipulated that anybody who failed to come to work for anything between three and five days could be fired, their jobs could be terminated for that reason.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you continue working for the ministry?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I continued working until the beginning of March 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why did you cease working at that point?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation became more complicated by the day. There were a lot more incidents happening. The roads were blocked and I couldn't get to Selo [phoen] from Hadzici and Pazarici. Nobody guaranteed my safety in the building of the ministry. I was even suggested by my colleagues, primarily by my friends, with whom I was on friendly terms even before, that I would be better off not coming to work at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were living with your family at this point in time in Hadzici; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in Hadzici, but some ten to 20 -- 12 kilometres further from Hadzici, closer to a place called Pazaric.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your home was in which municipality, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The municipality was Hadzici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, could I just ask one clarifying question? You said that the situation slowly deteriorated. Do you remember what was the last day that you went to work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't remember the date but I remember that it was at the beginning of March 1992. I can't give you the exact date, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that was when the roads were blocked already? Did you ever go to work passing through these roadblocks or were they erected after you went to work for the last time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Barricades had been put up much earlier on some of the roads. Sometimes I was lucky and I didn't have any problems passing through those barricades, but the situation was getting more complicated, it was very dangerous, and there were lot of risks to be taken. At that time, in Ilidza, which is a municipality next to Hadzici on the way to Sarajevo, there had already been incidents, there had already been dead and killed. There had been conflicts. I don't know whether it was March or in April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kapetina, you answered my question. Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You -- there came a point in time where you decided to move your family out of the area. When was that, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I decided to move out my family to a safer place towards the end of April, on the eve of the 1st of May. The last day of April, the 30th of April, that is, I decided to move my wife and two children out and I drove them to a safer location.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the period from the point in time when you had ceased working in Sarajevo, to the point in time that you removed your family from the area, what if anything were you doing in Hadzici?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: From mid-March to the 30th of April, when I finally left the municipality of Hadzici and my place of residence, I volunteered in Hadzici. In Hadzici there was an Assembly of the Serbian People and I was elected deputy president of that assembly. This was not a professional duty. I worked as a volunteer. In addition to the president and deputy, there was also a council of that assembly which consisted of the most prominent Serbs in Hadzici. That council numbered 20 Serbian intellectuals from Hadzici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not going to ask you very much about what happened in Hadzici at that particular time. But there is one topic I do want to question you in relation to, and that is this: Were you aware of Muslims departing from the municipality?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Towards the end of April, I noticed, as I drove to Hadzici in my own vehicle, that Muslims were leaving the territory of Hadzici. They were leaving the area in tractors and trailers. They even tied their cattle to those tractors. They moved out slowly in those tractors, to Tarcin and Pazarici. Towards the end of April this was not happening on a very large scale, but every day somebody would move out in that direction. I'm talking only about the Muslim population of Hadzici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any idea why they were doing this?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assumed that this was all being done for safety reasons. However, it may have even been organised. There may have even been a plan to do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to come back to that in a moment but I think it would help if we continued with your own chronology of events. You've told us that on the 30th of April, you left the municipality of Hadzici. Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I just happened to receive a confirmation from the leadership of that municipality that I could use 50 litres of fuel. Before that I had always used my own fuel and then I decided to use that fuel to move my family out from the territory of that place where I had resided. Obviously my parents stayed behind in our family house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it right - I think I can summarise this - that having deposited your family in a safe place, you attempted some days later to return to Hadzici but you were unable to because of roadblocks? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I intended to go back to Hadzici. I decided to move my family because some of my colleagues from that council had done the same. They had sent their families to Montenegro or Serbia and I felt an obligation towards my family to do the same. And it was my intention once this was done to return to Hadzici. However, due to very serious roadblocks, which were not just sporadic barricades but full blockades on the roads, I could not go back to Hadzici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to stop your chronology at that point, and I want to look at a few documents with you. Firstly, and I appreciate that this is untranslated.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I very much doubt whether I will seek to have all of this document translated. Could we look at tab 1, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a document consisting of almost 60 pages, and if we look at page 1, which is the one that is open there, we see your name, Dragan Kapetina. Could you read the other words on that page, please, for the record?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Manual for drawing up plans in emergency conditions."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a manual that you wrote in 1990; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was part of your work in the ministry; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I want you to summarise its purpose, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The law on all people's Defence, both the federal as well as the republican law, prescribed an obligation that all those who were subject to those laws had to draw up not only their peacetime plans but also plans for extraordinary circumstances and conditions. I, as a republican inspector, felt an obligation to interpret the provisions of the laws that regulated that area, and I'm talking about the regulations of the Presidency of the SFRY and the decision of the federal council, to interpret them and to clarify them for those who were subject to drawing up those plans that were a legal obligation that they had to honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the details and information contained within this manual, where did you gather and collate the material from? In absolute outline, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used the provisions of the federal and republican laws. I also used the regulations that existed at the federal level, that was passed by the Presidency of the SFRY, as well as the decision of the federal council on the methodology of drawing up such plans. Since those regulations were not very detailed, I decided to explain in practical terms how to draw up each and every document that was part and parcel of those plans. I used my personal experience because on behalf of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I had participated in drawing up federal laws and regulations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you now take a look, please, at tab 2?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, I noticed that the rather extensive document under tab 1 is not translated, and I do not exactly know that apart from perhaps it comes down to tab 2 but doesn't seem to be perhaps directly -- perhaps it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well perhaps -- I did say a moment ago that it wasn't translated, conceded that it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I would have thought that resources would dictate that having this translated would be almost impossible, but perhaps we could come back to that situation when I've concluded this topic. Your Honour will see in a few moments where I'm heading with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I can imagine what it is but let's just wait and hear from the witness what his answers to your questions are. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tab 2 is a document this Court is extremely familiar with. Listen to my question carefully, Mr. Kapetina.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I should say for the record I think it's part of P64 headed instructions for the organisation, operation of organs, the Serbian people of Bosnia-Herzegovina in emergency conditions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My first question to you is we see this document is dated 19th of December 1991. Did you see it in and around that time, in other words either in late 1991 or in 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see this document either towards the end of 1991 or after that. The first time I saw this document was when I was interviewed by the investigators of the Prosecutor's office of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just stop there. It is right, isn't it, that on the 14th of May, and I think also a date in July of 2004, you were interviewed under what I call a caution, by, as you've said, investigators and indeed lawyers of the Office of the Prosecutor, that interview taking place at their Sarajevo field office? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were interviewed for many hours and you answered all the questions that they asked you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. The interview was taken over two days, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you've just told us that the first time you saw this document in tab 2 was when the investigators showed it to you? You have just said that, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it is right, isn't it, that they put to you that there were similarities between the document at tab 2 and the document in tab 1, the one that you drafted; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My next question is: Having read in detail the text of the document in tab 2, is it a document that you find surprising or worrying in any way?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have read the document. I read it now while preparing for testimony, and I wasn't surprised by it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why weren't you surprised by it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a moment ago, in answering another question, I said that the federal law on total national defence and the republican law on total national defence provided for possible situations that a country can face and the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina as well. In addition to a state of war and imminent danger of war, the law proscribed for emergency situations, and in keeping with those legal provisions and the definition of a state of emergency, and I don't think that was only the situation in socialist Yugoslavia because in other countries and systems, there are situations of crisis and emergency situations as well. Anyway, two federal provisions were enacted that I mentioned a moment ago, guidelines by the SFRY for eliminating emergency situations and a government decision by the federal executive council on the methods for compiling plans for emergency situations, and in conformity with those two provisions and the law on national defence for Bosnia-Herzegovina, all the subjects and protagonists in the planning process were duty-bound to devise and compile plans for emergency situations. And I am linking up that document now with that obligation under the law. So the political party was the subject of planning in the former socialist Yugoslavia. And therefore probably because of the overall situation in the republic itself, and probably in the party itself, this kind of set of instructions were compiled as had been presented to me here today. And I'd like to say another thing once we are analysing this document. And it is this: According to these instructions, there are certain measures, activities and tasks provided for but if you take a look at the document in its entirety then you'll see that they have just been listed, without being actually ordered. No orders have been issued. And so at the end of this document, I don't know in what point, perhaps it was point 3, it says quite literally that the person compiling the instructions will order when and where each measure would be undertaken. So that is why I said that I see nothing particularly surprising in this document. It can be considered as legally binding and the result of the overall situation in the republic, if you will, now I don't know what the situation was like in the party itself, but this segment still does not comprise measures that were ordered but measures that could be potentially ordered for execution. That's what I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what do you say to the assertion put to you by the Office of the Prosecutor's investigators that the document that you wrote, the manual that we find at tab 1, is similar to the document at tab 2?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my interview with the investigators, I understood it that they, on the basis of my notebook for the elaboration of the plans, arrived at the idea that I could have been one of the authors working on these instructions. That's how I understood it. And I categorically rejected any links with this document of myself as an author and I explained this by saying that in my aide-memoire, I explained this subject matter far more professionally and in greater details so that it is quite obvious that I was not the author of this document, nor did I know about it. Had I implemented the process of supervision I would have come across this document in the municipality, had it existed at the time. That's what I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I now would like to turn, please, to tab 3 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, just as far as relevance is concerned, of course, we never know what to expect but you've now spent quite some time on a denial that Mr. Kapetina might have been the author of the 19th of December instructions. No one ever suggested that up until this moment, as far as I'm aware of. So therefore it's fine to know that you could call a couple of other witnesses telling that they are not or asking them whether they would deny authorship of this. I wonder, the only thing that happens it suddenly comes into my mind that people may have thought Mr. Kapetina was and then to digest that and to say that there are now good reasons to accept that, just on the basis of their thoughts. But you're telling us at least until now --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I don't follow Your Honour. Your Honour puts it slightly differently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What I understand your line of questioning is that it may ever have been suggested to Mr. Kapetina, whether clear or not, I do not know the document, I haven't seen the interview so no one ever gave us any material to suggest to us that Mr. Kapetina would have been the author, and then you've spent some time on exploring that he could not have been because otherwise he would have seen the 19th of December sections, of course, at an earlier stage. I wonder what's the use.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Ah, first of all, Your Honour doesn't get the interview because I'm not permitted to put that before the Court and I'm not seeking at this juncture to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apart from that --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That wasn't the purpose of this evidence. The purpose of the evidence did not relate to the authorship or otherwise by this witness of that document. The purpose --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it is similarity.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I sense that there is some caution on Mr. Josse's part in enunciating the purpose of the evidence so that he doesn't specifically indicate to the witness who is now giving testimony what his purpose is, which would be rather akin to a leading question. I appreciate that. If he's going to be asked to continue to explain --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it should be in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's half of it. There is a bit more to it as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps it would take more time than it would bring us. So let's forget about it for a moment. But at least I gave you the impression I gained from some of the previous questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That was not the purpose of this -- these questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Hanoteau would like to address something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask the witness to tell me the following. This document on tab 1, was this document published? We don't really understand very clearly. Mr. Josse, you've talked about a manual, a book. What was the purpose of this document? Why was it drafted? Who asked for this document to be drafted? To whom was this document given, this manual given? Why was it drafted? Why was it prepared? Why was it made? Could you please answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can answer all of those questions, can't you, Mr. Kapetina? And I invite you to do so, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear the question. This manual was printed in 5.000 copies. The number of copies that there were planning subjects in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And the manual was distributed to each of the subjects or protagonists in the planning process. Of course, this was authorised by the republican secretary for national defence which was a General Muharem Tepahagic [phoen] at the time. Considering that this was a good manual which could be of assistance to the subjects to compile and comply with their legal obligations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I've invited your attention to tab 3, please. This is an extract from a book by a Sefer Halilovic called Cunning Strategy; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. That's the document I have before me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you have had a chance to read this particular chapter; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Just this chapter. The chapter that has been presented here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I have two questions. The first is: Does this in any way help you to explain the activities of the Muslims of Hadzici that you have already mentioned, namely their departure?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Among other things, that too. Although there are other things as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us first of all about that issue and then we can turn to the other matters.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have been given this portion of the book and the title is Tasks of the Regional Military Staff, and directives for the defence of the sovereignty of the author Sefer Halilovic, for the defence of sovereignty. I'd like to remind the Chamber and ask them to look at point 2, the tasks of the regional military staff. At the end of point 2, it states the following: "Plan, from which areas, villages and local commune the Muslim population would be evacuated, the line of withdrawal, who will secure it, reception areas, and accommodation. Plan how to secure federal and republican resources of supplies -- reserves of supplies."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is the significance of that, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said a moment ago that I thought to begin with that the people for security reasons and their safety was being moved out or was moving out, and that was the logical conclusion because everybody values their own personal safety and the safety of their families above all else. However, I assumed that there was planned moving out as well, and here we have it. In reading these tasks, this confirms my suspicions and conviction that the dislocation which in Bosnia-Herzegovina is often taken to mean ethnic cleansing were in fact planned actions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you found other parts of this chapter significant. In what way?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think -- I don't think the Court will mind but let me say that I'm sorry to say that -- I'm sorry that I hadn't read the book earlier, but what is set out in these two or three pages is truly surprising or astounding, in fact. On page 11, for instance, you can understand one could understand that these activities tombs in the second half of 1991, that is to say preparations for the meeting held on the 7th and 8th of February, which was a consultation of regional staffs, the commanders of regional staffs in actual fact and preparations for that meeting were conducted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Reference to page 11 where I've got five pages. Could you -- or is it in the B/C/S original and we have to find --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's 11 at the top, Your Honour. In fact it's the very first page, I think, the introduction which says on the 7th of February 1992. For some reason it says 11 on the top of that page. It's 11 in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Next page gives 11, bottom down, bottom so I do understand. It's the very first part. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. In fact, the tasks of regional military staffs, that text was come pied at the end of 1991, which is astounding. If we read to the end the tasks set out in eight points, then I'd like to draw your attention to point 2 once again, where it states the following: The disposition of our units, strength and composition, possible planned operation, if necessary a way to block the barracks, the way to attack the stockpiles in order to seize weapons or simply to block them. Mark places of buildings envisaged for sabotage, mark precisely the towns or sectors for municipal logistic bases and regional logistic bases. I read out the following sentence which says "plan from which areas," et cetera. And it's also interesting to note point 1, which addresses the disposition of SDS units. And the second portion of point 1 is particularly interesting where it says "mark on the map the ethnic structure of villages, municipalities, urban and suburban settlements," and then in brackets, Muslim and Croatian villages, a complete green circle with the letter C beside the Croatian villages, S -- and a blue circle beside Serbian villages. This bears out the thesis according to my minister that we are the blues, that is to say the enemy side, which is confirmed in Mr. Halilovic's book because he refers to Serb villages and says a blue circle. So all the other areas are marked in green, a green circle. I don't want to comment on what the green circle signifies but it says, or Sefer Halilovic says put a C for Croatian villages or H for Hrvatska, and I will tell you why. There was an attempt to make a unified organised armed force from the Territorial Defence but once again without the Serbs, minus the Serbs, and the Croats didn't agree to that. Mr. Halilovic and the political leadership of the SDA was left nothing else but to form a paramilitary in this way and that was the Patriotic League. While I'm analysing this document, I'd like to draw your attention further to another document entitled or the second part of the document entitled, "Directive for the defence of sovereignty," especially the portion speaking of the overall enemy forces and we can see the combined forces of the enemy and who the enemy is considered to be in Bosnia-Herzegovina. It says here that the SDS forces --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Just fop for a moment. I was simply going to get you to clarify that that's the handwritten document, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger has another point.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I may have to check the 65 ter summary but while I understood the witness would be making reference to this document, what appears to be happening is a kind of quasi-attempted expert analysis that would normally be the subject of a great deal more notice than has been provided in this case, leaving me in the position of attempting to parse out what is personal knowledge, what is opinion, to delve into the basis, all of which seems -- it seems like we are drifting very close to, if not already over the line, of the distinction between a witness who offers either personal knowledge or appropriate kinds of generalised opinions and into something far more. And I -- at this point, I'm concerned about the level of analysis that the Defence is seeking to elicit based on the information that was indicated previously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, as usual I was anxious, Your Honour, not to lead. Perhaps I could deal specifically with the matter which I did give Mr. Tieger notice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Let me first give a brief response to what I consider not an objection but a concern of Mr. Tieger. The Chamber might think that the analysis is not an in-depth analysis of the situation. The witness draws our attention to the fact that SDS units are mentioned while even without him drawing the attention to it we might have noticed that anyhow, carefully reading this document, so I might not be that much concerned at this moment as to the expert knowledge needed for the observations the witness made. At the same time, that might diminish also the value of his answers. So therefore it's a very good suggestion, as you said, that you would now turn to the subject specifically mentioned in the summary, but I suggest that you do that after the break because I take it you'll not be finished with it in two minutes. We'll have a break until quarter past six.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. As apparently has become our custom in the new Courtroom II, I would like to begin with a very quick housekeeping matter. That is with respect to tab 17 advise the court that the document from which Mr. Harmon read and which should have been placed in tab 17 is, in fact, P188. I have copies of that here and can distribute it as soon as we -- at the end of the session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So that's then on the record. And the quote finally found its source. Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think for Mr. Kapetina's benefit he's looking we bewildered. It's got nothing to do with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. This was a matter entirely different from your testimony. I should have explained that to you first. Thank you for reminding me, Mr. Josse. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I deal with a semi-housekeeping matter that is relevant to Mr. Kapetina's evidence. Can I call -- can I inform the Court that if we look at tab 3, if we look at the B/C/S, there is the handwritten document at page 167, at the bottom right-hand corner. The Court will see that that document has two lines through it creating a cross effect. Those lines have been put there by us, the reason being we were not inviting the CLSS to translate them. In fact, most of that document is translated, I suspect because it had previously been translated. I have no doubt for -- for Mr. Halilovic's trial, among other things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now you see how unfamiliar we are with these kind of books. I got the impression that someone who drafted this memo in handwriting and later disagreed or wanted to get rid of it, and struck it through.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I add, tomorrow, I hope, I will replace that page. I'm relying on Mr. Krajisnik's library and he's kindly agreed to lend me the book for that purpose tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I ask for a number whilst on this subject, for tab 3, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 3, Your Honours, will be D120.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the last question I want to ask you in relation to this extract from Mr. Halilovic's book is this, Mr. Kapetina. Are there any similarities that you see between what Mr. Halilovic is advocating in these pages and what you read in the document in tab 2, dealing with emergency conditions?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very briefly. There is a huge difference. I said that in there, measures and tasks are just listed, and there there is a passive relationship there. They are not ordered. They only should be ordered or not ordered for that matter. In this document here, however, by Mr. Sefer Halilovic, these are the command documents, directives and tasks. These are command documents. And it is astonishing under item 4 where he says, "I have decided." This is a command document. As he says here, he already has under his command 120.000 people. And finally, those forces that are ascribed to the SDS, the JNA, actually, this is not the enemy. This is the only legitimate and legal force in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the only armed force. And just for a better understanding, the largest unit in the Sarajevo corps that Mr. Halilovic ranges as enemy is under the command of Mr. Rasim Delic, a general who would later on become his superior.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As I said I will, I'm now going to move on and return to your activities. You've told us that you were unable to return to Hadzici. You've explained why. Where did you go instead?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I arrived from Serbia, from Vrsic [phoen] where I had left my family. I arrived in Pale because that was the only possible road. The road Bijeljina -- actually, Belgrade-Bijeljina-Zvornik, and then onwards to Sokolac and Pale. Thus I arrived in Pale.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you first arrived there, what was your intention? Why did you go there? You've explained why it is you ended up there but did you intend to stay there for long? What were you hoping to do thereafter?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to go back to Hadzici. That was my intention. However, the combat activities had already started there. There was very clear border between the area under the control of the Muslims and the area under the control of the Serbs. At first I could not even reach the area that was under the control of Serbs which was the centre of Hadzici and as for my place of residence, until the very end of the war it remained under the control of the Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I think, rather than deal at this precise moment with what you did in Pale, bearing in mind your last answer, could we deal with another topic that flows from your last answer, albeit quite briefly. What happened at this point in time to your parents?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At first I did not have any information as to what was happening to my parents. My father and mother were there. It was only towards the end of June that I learned that all the men in Tarcin and Pazarici had been incarcerated in the silo in Tarcin, that a camp had been formed there for Serbs aging in range from 17 to 70 years of age. Later on, this information was completed by the fact that my father was among the 700 or 800 incarcerated Serbs. It was only later that I learned that he was not incarcerated because he was my father but because he was a Serb because all the Serbs were incarcerated there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think we - you should explain; it may be obvious - that the reason your father had been taken prisoner was because effectively he was living in the Muslim side of the line when the war actually started; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He found himself in the territory under the control of the Muslim forces. He was over 60 years of age at the time so he could not have been a soldier or a person carrying arms. All the men aged from 17 to 80 were incarcerated. Those things happened elsewhere as well but I can't bear the monstrous idea that people could be incarcerated in a silo with concrete walls, towering over 20 metres above people, and 700 to 800 men were incarcerated there and the sheer idea seems monstrous to me, to imprison people in a place like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your mother continued to live in her home but you were unable to have any contact with her, again because she was on the Muslim side of the line; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, she remained in our family house. She tried to help my father. She tried to take food to him. However, that food never reached him, and he died in November of that same year. He spent some five months in such horrific conditions. After that, my mother was exchanged and she moved to the area under the control of the Republika Srpska army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For the avoidance of any doubt, your father died whilst in custody in the silos?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My father died while he was in custody in the silos. He died due to the conditions that prevailed there, and the torture that he was subjected to. Not only him but the other people as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's move away from that sad subject and move to your life in Pale. What did you do when you got there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Bogdan Subotic was already there. I heard that he had been appointed the Defence Minister. Since I could not reach Hadzici and I happened to bump into my colleagues from the Ministry of Defence in Sarajevo, who had been in -- arrived in Pale before me, they told me to get in touch with minister Subotic just to see what was going on and whether I could be of any use to them. After having had my conversation with Subotic, he told me that I should urgently be engaged in the ministry as a professional. He was a minister and I was the only professional in Pale at the time. That was the Ministry of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, when we are talking about the headquarters in Pale. He was the minister and I was the only staffer. There was nobody else there but the two of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you start working under Mr. Subotic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know the exact date but I think it was after the 10th of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where was the offices of the ministry located?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time in May, there were no offices of the defence ministry. Actually, what there was was a room where Mr. Subotic worked and slept and I was in a sort of communal room and it was only at the beginning of June that the ministry and the other organs and the government as well were accommodated at the Bistica [phoen] hotel on Mount Jahorina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to give the Court some idea of the development of the ministry, you've told us that when you started working there, you and Mr. Subotic were the only people working in that department; that's right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. And I'd like to stress again and to explain that as far as the headquarters of the ministry at Pale was concerned, that was how it was. The others were municipal organs for National Defence on the territory under the control of the army of Republika Srpska and within the composition of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So all the municipality Secretariats continued working. Of course, we didn't have ties with many of them but that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many people were working in the ministry at the time it was moved or housed in the hotel on Mount Jahorina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The number of people working there varied but it was between 10 and 15 at the most.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your role or job within the ministry, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our prime job was after the assembly was held of the Serb people in Banja Luka, which elected and formed the army of Republika Srpska in actual fact, was to prepare a law on defence and law on the army for the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That was the first task we were given so we undertook to draft those two laws. The army was also supposed to prepare the law and draft the law for the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, to some extent, that last answer deals with the question I'm about to ask you, but the law on the army, to what degree were you involved in its drafting?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was involved on the draft -- drafting the law on defence. I didn't work on the law for the army. That was done by the soldiers. And it followed the assembly held in Banja Luka. During that period of time, immediately after the assembly, that is, we took urgent measures to prepare three provisions dealing with respect for international war law, and we prepared an order already on the 13th of May for respect of the international human rights, international conduct with respect to prisoners of war, and with respect to the Geneva Conventions. All those three provisions were drafted and prepared by the end of May 1992. And all those three wartime provisions were sent up to the Main Staff, the corps command, and the command of the Main Staff issued an order with respect to the implementation of those instructions and guidelines. All that was printed and then sent out to almost every single soldier in the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you turn to tab 6, please? This is an extract from the Official Gazette of the Serb people in Bosnia-Herzegovina. In the -- they had previously been exhibited on, we think, three occasions in this case, P64, 65, 529. In fact, as the Court will see, in the English, there are two completely separate translations but in the B/C/S, they form one document, 156 and 157 of the gazette. I first want to ask you about number 157, please. This is a lengthy document running to 84 articles. It's signed by Dr. Karadzic, 1st of June 1992, in the gazette of the same day. Is this the law on defence that you were just telling us about that you were primarily responsible for drafting?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. That's it. That's the text of the law. Although, you can't be the author or have authorship over a law. A law is enacted by the authorities authorised to do so but, yes, that's the draft that we prepared.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, for our presentation, we have not included the history of this law, and I appreciate that you were involved in drafting it some years ago. But in absolute summary, what documents did you use, if you can remember, in order to prepare it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the basis for this law was the previous law on total national defence for Bosnia-Herzegovina. And for the most part, we endeavoured to proscribe the position and role of all the state organs of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and their competences and authorisations in the field of defence. As I say, the basis was the law that was in force previously, the law on total national defence in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And in one of the ash tickles we say that an army established in that way by the assembly would be regulated by a separate law. Of course, this law on defence had already established the chain of command for the defence and army of Republika Srpska by the president of the republic or rather from the level of president of the republic right down to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you involved in any of the political mechanics in organising the passing of this law by the Serb assembly?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not directly involved in any political activities. I already emphasised that. This law was passed urgently because that's what the situation was like. The Muslim-Croatian coalition proclaimed a state of war in Bosnia-Herzegovina and a decision was passed in Sarajevo to form the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, so all in all, there were not many political activities preceding this law. There was a demand to pass the law and to regulate the most urgent matters which were the position of all the institutions, the state institutions in defence and to regulate the overall relationships in the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like, please, now, to have a look at number 156 in the same gazette, please. This is the law on amending the constitutional law for implementing the constitution of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it relates to a decision about War Presidencies. Were you involved in drafting this law?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, before the witness proceeds, I would benefit from some direction. I have been in tab 6, following the discussion about the law on defence, and now the reference to number 156 has not assisted me in finding the document to which counsel is now referring.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This, in my version of the bundle, is the very first document in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's a two-page document from what I see, page numbers 27 and 28, handwritten tab 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So my question, Mr. Kapetina, was whether you were involved in the drafting of this law.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I wasn't involved in the drafting of this other law. But I was aware of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was your understanding of what it meant?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I have learned to read laws. I know what a norm is and in my view it says in the article one in this law that it is only during a state of war that the Presidency is expanded with the following members that are listed herein. And since in the Srpska Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina no state of war was proclaimed, or at least not during the passing of this law, then this remained just a possibility. If a state of war was ever declared, then the Presidency could be expanded by the following officials, the president of the national assembly and the Prime Minister of the government.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it may be an obvious question but why do you say that a state of war was never declared? What -- put another way, what does the term "state of war" mean?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the law defines who is it who proclaims a state of war. And if that person, who is authorised or that body that is authorised, which is the parliament or, when it cannot assemble it is the president of the republic, and if such a state has not been proclaimed by them then such a state does not exist. A state of war can only exist if it has been proclaimed as such by the body or the person authorised to do so by the law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as you were concerned, as a person working both in Pale and in particular in the Ministry of Defence, was there an expanded Presidency in Republika Srpska in 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Republika Srpska, in keeping with the constitution and laws, there was just a Presidency, and the composition of the Presidency was clearly defined, a president and two vice-presidents. That was the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. There was no expanded presidency, as an institution. Later on, there was the president of the republic or the chair person or the president of the Presidency and then just the president of the republic. This is the chronology: First there was a three-member Presidency, and then there was a Presidency with one president and two vice-presidents, and finally when Republika Srpska was established, then the president of the republic was appointed. There was never any appointed Presidency especially not in the situation of an immediate threat of war. It is always very clearly defined by the law that an independent individual person is in charge of the army, rather than a collective body. It is not possible for a collective body to be in charge of commanding. I am very well aware of that detail because I had to be aware who it is who issues commands to whom and when.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let's turn to that issue, since you've raised it. Who did command the army in 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992, immediately when the army was established, at the same session or the session after that, instead of the Presidency, it was the chairperson of the Presidency, Mr. Radovan Karadzic, who was put in command of the army. Later on, until the moment the president was appointed, he was still in command of the army, but acting as the president of the republic. During the month of January, February, March, and April, under the law, it was the three-member Presidency that was in command. The president, two vice-presidents, but at that time we did not have an army. Our army was just on paper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are you able to give any opinion, again bearing in mind the position that you held, of the actual influence the people you have just mentioned had over the Serb -- well, the army of the people fighting on behalf of the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that all these people that performed those duties had reputation among the people, among the troops - I'm talking about the president and two vice-presidents - and this reputation was unquestionable. There were some other individuals who -- whose influence was adequate to the position they held in their respective institutions. Of course, the civil -- civilian command had the most influence over the army, because it bore the highest responsibility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll deal with one specific matter now, if I may. Tab 7. These are -- previously have been exhibited. According to our records, P64, P65, P583, minutes from the 22nd government, meeting of the Serb republic held on the 7th of June 1992. And I want you to turn, please, to the last page in the B/C/S version. I want you to look at decree four, the penultimate page in the English. It says the requests of corps and hospital to use the supplies found in the building in which the hospital what housed has been accepted. Where was the Koran hospital, first of all?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in Pale. It used to be a hotel before that. When I arrived in Pale, that hotel was already used as a hospital, a hospital that was used to treat wounded and injured soldiers and civilians. It was already as of the 10th of May when I arrived in Pale, that the hotel Koran had already been turned into a hospital and it was used as a hospital until the very end of the war. And I claim that with full certainty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you say to the suggestion that this place, the Koran, was used to detain either enemy combatants or enemy civilians?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only that place or that building, I never heard information, and I was well informed about the situation in Pale, that in Pale, there was any sort of prison for any sort of prisoners. We did not even have a prison for members of our own army, those who breached discipline. I claim with full responsibility that in Pale, while I was there, there was no prison there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally on this, are you able to comment at all about what it actually says there, namely the request of the hospital to use the supplies found within the building? Do you know anything about that specifically?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if that was a hotel, and indeed it was a hotel, that means that there were some leftovers that the hotel had used for its guests. The government was required to issue a decision to allow the hospital to use all those goods. There would be a subsequent compensation for that. Those were not a -- state reserves. Those goods and leftovers were property of the hotel, and a decision should be issued to the effect of allowing the hospital to use them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Would that be a convenient moment, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it would. Could you give us an indication, Mr. Josse, on how much time you would still need?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. I would now be surprised if I went beyond the first session tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the witness was scheduled for?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think six hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Six hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think I'm going to be rather less than that. That's my present estimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, fine. Then we will adjourn for the day. I'd like to instruct you, Mr. Kapetina, not to speak with anyone about the testimony you have given until now, neither to speak with anyone about the testimony still to be given in the days to come. We would like to see you back tomorrow in this same courtroom at a quarter past two. We stand adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 18th day of January, 2006, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.01 p.m.,
